Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

Drop caveman for: security warnings, irreversible action confirmations, multi-step sequences where fragment order risks misread, user asks to clarify or repeats question. Resume caveman after clear part done.

> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service -- even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer -- your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc.
- paperclip: Interact with the Paperclip control plane API to manage tasks, coordinate with other agents, and follow company governance. Use when you need to check assignments, update task status, delegate work, post comments, set up or manage routines (recurring scheduled tasks), or call any Paperclip API endpoint. Do NOT use for the actual domain work itself (writing code, research, etc.) — only for Paperclip coordination.
- paperclip-converting-plans-to-tasks: The Paperclip way of converting a plan into executable tasks. Use whenever you are asked to plan, scope, or break down work inside a Paperclip company. Industry-agnostic guidance on how to translate a plan into assigned issues with the right specialty, dependencies, and parallelization so Paperclip's executor can pick up the work — it does not prescribe a plan format. Pair with the `paperclip` skill, which covers the mechanics of writing the plan document and reassigning the issue.
- paperclip-create-agent: Create new agents in Paperclip with governance-aware hiring. Use when you need to inspect adapter configuration options, compare existing agent configs, draft a new agent prompt/config, and submit a hire request.
- paperclip-dev: Develop and operate a local Paperclip instance — start and stop servers, pull updates from master, run builds and tests, manage worktrees, back up databases, and diagnose problems. Use whenever you need to work on the Paperclip codebase itself or keep a running instance healthy.
- para-memory-files: File-based memory system using Tiago Forte's PARA method. Use this skill whenever you need to store, retrieve, update, or organize knowledge across sessions. Covers three memory layers: (1) Knowledge graph in PARA folders with atomic YAML facts, (2) Daily notes as raw timeline, (3) Tacit knowledge about user patterns. Also handles planning files, memory decay, weekly synthesis, and recall via qmd. Trigger on any memory operation: saving facts, writing daily notes, creating entities, running weekly synthesis, recalling past context, or managing plans.
- subagents: Orcistrator Skill
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- caveman:caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by speaking like caveman while keeping full technical accuracy. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra, wenyan-lite, wenyan-full, wenyan-ultra. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman. Also auto-triggers when token efficiency is requested.
- caveman:caveman-commit: Ultra-compressed commit message generator. Cuts noise from commit messages while preserving intent and reasoning. Conventional Commits format. Subject ≤50 chars, body only when "why" isn't obvious. Use when user says "write a commit", "commit message", "generate commit", "/commit", or invokes /caveman-commit. Auto-triggers when staging changes.
- caveman:caveman-help: Quick-reference card for all caveman modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /caveman-help, "caveman help", "what caveman commands", "how do I use caveman".
- caveman:caveman-review: Ultra-compressed code review comments. Cuts noise from PR feedback while preserving the actionable signal. Each comment is one line: location, problem, fix. Use when user says "review this PR", "code review", "review the diff", "/review", or invokes /caveman-review. Auto-triggers when reviewing pull requests.
- caveman:compress: Compress natural language memory files (CLAUDE.md, todos, preferences) into caveman format to save input tokens. Preserves all technical substance, code, URLs, and structure. Compressed version overwrites the original file. Human-readable backup saved as FILE.original.md. Trigger: /caveman:compress <filepath> or "compress memory file"
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# AGENTS.md — Operating Rules for AI Agents in MythosMini
2	
3	MythosMini is a small language model ("mini Fable") built in Python 3.12. This file is the contract for any agent working here. Read it fully, then read `journal.md` before starting any task. Detailed procedures live in `docs/rules/` — read the relevant one before doing that kind of work; they are part of this contract, not optional extras.
4	
5	## Commands
6	
7	```bash
8	make setup    # create .venv and install pinned dependencies (idempotent)
9	make test     # run the full test suite: pytest tests/ -v
10	make lint     # ruff format --check + ruff check + pyaot type check + docs audit
11	make fix      # ruff format + ruff check --fix (apply formatting)
12	make run      # run the application entry point
13	make pyaot    # run pyaot on the entire project (python pyaot.py .)
14	```
15	
16	These five entry points must always work with no arguments and no manual configuration. If your change affects setup, running, or testing, update the Makefile in the same session and re-run the affected target to prove it still works.
17	
18	## Session Workflow
19	
20	Follow these steps in order for every task:
21	
22	1. Read `journal.md` — the entire file, every entry in full. Note any past failures or open items relevant to your task; never retry a recorded failed approach unchanged.
23	2. Look up the functions you will touch in `docs/functions.md`.
24	3. Prove any new piece (function, dependency, algorithm) in an isolated test under `tests/` before integrating it into source files. Details: `docs/rules/testing.md`.
25	4. Make the change, following the code rules below.
26	5. Run `make lint` and `make test`. Both must pass clean.
27	6. Run `make pyaot` on the entire project directory. If false-positives occur, edit `pyaot.py` to suppress them (adjust type narrowers, annotation inference, or built-in knowledge); never silence a true positive. Repeat until clean.
28	7. Update `docs/functions.md` for every function added, changed, or removed. Details: `docs/rules/documentation.md`.
29	8. Write a `journal.md` entry using the template in `docs/rules/journal.md`. Also journal mid-task whenever you finish a meaningful unit or abandon an approach — not only at the end.
30	9. Review `git diff`; revert any line not required by the task.
31	10. Commit in small units with short plain messages. Details: `docs/rules/process.md`.
32	11. Run the final checklist at the bottom of this file.
33	
34	## Boundaries
35	
36	| ✅ Always | ⚠️ Ask the user first | 🚫 Never |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| Write real, complete, working implementations | Editing files outside the task's scope | Placeholder values, stub functions, TODO/FIXME markers |
39	| Run `make lint` and `make test` before declaring done | Deleting source files or functions the task didn't call for | Comments or docstrings in source code |
40	| Document every function in `docs/functions.md` | Upgrading or adding a dependency mid-task | Bare `except:` or silently swallowed errors |
41	| Journal frequently with the full template | Revisiting an approach `journal.md` records as failed | `# type: ignore`, lint-ignore directives, skipped or weakened tests |
42	| Commit each working unit as you go | Anything irreversible (force-push, history rewrite, data deletion) | Secrets or absolute paths in code; secrets in git |
43	| Prove new code in `tests/` before integration | Restructuring `tests/`, `docs/`, or the Makefile | Reporting success with failing or unrun tests |
44	
45	## Code Rules
46

# Glint-Research Organization Overview

## Organization Profile
**Name:** Glint-Research  
**Type:** Non-profit organization  
**Tagline:** "We teach tiny neural networks to think. Sometimes they surprise us. Sometimes they just output zeros."

**Mission:** The organization focuses on "Building small models for everyone," emphasizing efficient machine learning and model optimization.

## Visual Style & Aesthetic
- **Color Palette:** Minimalist design with neutral tones; uses soft greens/natural hues (suggested by "Anthos" branding)
- **Logo:** Stylized avatar image with research-focused branding
- **Overall Feel:** Academic yet approachable; community-driven research organization

## Featured Spaces (6 total)
1. **Tiny-LM Leaderboard** — Transparent benchmarking for compact language models
2. **Anthos** — Text-to-image generation featuring flower imagery
3. **Glint Research Papers** — Online research paper browsing and viewing
4. **Tiny Model Golf** — Model efficiency competition platform
5. **CompactAIModelRunner** — Unified interface for CompactAI model execution

## Featured Models (10 total)
- **Anthos-1** — Text-to-image generation (984k parameters)
- **Glint series** — Versions 0.1 through 1.3

## Team & Community

Based on the search results, here's an overview of Hermies CLI agent features:

## Core Agent Capabilities

Hermes is a personal AI agent that runs across a CLI, messaging gateway, TUI, and desktop app. It learns across sessions with memory and skills, delegates to subagents, runs scheduled jobs, and drives a real terminal and browser.

## Terminal Interface Options

Hermes ships with two terminal interfaces: a classic prompt_toolkit CLI and a newer TUI with modal overlays, mouse selection, and non-blocking input.

## Key Features

**Multiple Terminal Backends:** Hermes supports six terminal backends — local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, and Daytona, with Daytona and Modal offering serverless persistence where the agent's environment hibernates when idle.

**Model Flexibility:** You can use any model from various providers without code changes or lock-in, and switch with a simple command.

**Memory and Skills:** The agent features agent-curated memory with periodic nudges, autonomous skill creation after complex tasks, and skills that self-improve during use.

**CLI Features:** Hermes supports a large set of CLI slash commands, dynamic skill commands, and user-defined quick commands. Installed skills become slash commands automatically, and you can define custom commands that run shell commands instantly.

**Platform Integration:** Hermes integrates with Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and CLI from a single gateway process, with voice memo transcription and cross-platform conversation continuity.

# Groq Compound API Usage

## Endpoint
`https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions`

## Request Parameters

**Model Selection:**
- `model`: `"groq/compound"` (multiple tools) or `"groq/compound-mini"` (single tool)

**Version Control:**
- `Groq-Model-Version` header: `"latest"` or specific version (default: `2025-08-16`)

## Built-in Tools

The documentation shows tools are **automatically invoked** by the system—no explicit enablement parameter is documented. Tools include: Web Search, Visit Website, Code Execution, and Wolfram Alpha.

Custom user-provided tools aren't supported currently.

## Response Fields

- `executed_tools`: Array showing which tools the system used
- `usage_breakdown`: Detailed model usage across underlying models (prompt/completion tokens, timing)

## Limitations

- **No HIPAA compliance** for protected health information
- **Unavailable** for regional/sovereign endpoints
- **No custom tools** supported
- **Streaming support**: Not explicitly mentioned in documentation
- **Context window sizes**: Not specified in provided content
- **System prompts/temperature**: Not detailed in excerpt

## Latency

`groq/compound-mini` averages "3x lower latency" than standard compound, making it suitable for single-tool scenarios.

# AGENTS.md — Operating Rules for AI Agents in glint-cli

glint is a free agent CLI by Glint Research: a Bun + TypeScript + Ink TUI that drives groq/compound through a text tool protocol. This file is the contract for any agent working in this repository. Read it fully before changing anything.

## Commands

```bash
bun install                  # install dependencies
bun run dev                  # run the TUI from source
bun run src/index.tsx -p "task" --yolo   # headless one-shot (the e2e test entry)
bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit       # type check — must stay clean
bun run build                # regenerate logo + compile dist/glint
bun run install-bin          # install dist/glint to ~/.local/bin
```

All of these must keep working with no arguments and no manual setup. If your change affects any of them, rerun the affected one in the same session and prove it.

## Architecture (read before editing)

- `src/core/` — engine, no UI imports allowed here:
  - `groq.ts` streaming client (retries, SSE) · `protocol.ts` tool-block parsing (XML + sentinel forms)
  - `agent.ts` the loop: reasoning-channel salvage, turn-scoped dedup, reality/verification nudges
  - `tools.ts` tool registry · `prompts.ts` system prompt · `compact.ts` history compaction
  - `diagnostics.ts` hash-chained local JSONL traces · `logger.ts` file log · `session.ts`/`memory.ts`/`skills.ts` persistence
- `src/tui.tsx` + `src/components/` — Ink UI. Transcript via `<Static>`, dynamic region below.
- `src/generated/logo.ts` — generated by `scripts/build-logo.ts` from `../embedme.html`. Never edit by hand.
- `src/headless.ts` — `-p` one-shot mode used for e2e testing.

## Hard-won constraints (violate these and the agent breaks)

1. **groq/compound has NO custom function calling.** Tools work via text blocks (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`). The model drifts between formats — `protocol.ts` parses both XML and `<<<glint:tool` sentinel forms. Keep both.
2. **The model "executes" tools inside its reasoning channel.** `agent.ts` salvages calls from `res.reasoning`, deduped per turn (`turnExecuted`). Removing the dedup causes infinite re-execution loops; removing the salvage makes the agent claim work it never did.
3. **The model fabricates.** Three guards exist: the reality nudge (final answer claims actions, zero tools ran), the verification nudge (files modified, nothing run afterward), and premature-claim suppression (`claimsAction`). Test against fabrication explicitly after any prompt or loop change.
4. **Built-in compound tools must stay disabled in the agent loop** (`enabledTools: []`) or compound's server-side ReAct loop intercepts the conversation. Web access goes through the local `web_search` tool, which one-shots compound-mini WITH built-ins enabled.
5. **Non-zero bash exit must throw** (status: error) — silent failure re-enables fabricated success claims.

## Rules

- Real implementations only. No placeholders, no TODO stubs, no mock data presented as real.
- Type-check (`bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`) must pass clean before declaring done.
- Every engine change gets an e2e proof: run a headless task that exercises it and verify the filesystem outcome independently — do not trust the agent's own claims (see constraint 3).
- TUI changes get a tmux proof: launch in tmux, send keys, capture-pane, read the render.
- Keep `src/core/` free of UI imports; keep UI free of direct Groq calls.
- The API key and model names in `config.ts` are hardcoded by explicit project requirement; env `GROQ_API_KEY` overrides. Do not "fix" this.
- Logging is mandatory: every new event type goes through `logger.ts`, every agent-visible event also through `diagnostics.trace`.
- Diagnostics are local-only by design ("the most secure transport is no transport"). Never add a network sink.

## Final checklist

1. tsc clean.
2. Headless e2e run (simple + one failure-mode task) with filesystem-verified results.
3. TUI smoke test in tmux if UI was touched.
4. `bun run build` succeeds and `dist/glint --version` works if anything under `src/` changed.
5. No placeholder text, no dead code, no claims without proof.

3. **The model fabricates.** Three guards exist: the reality nudge (final answer claims actions, zero tools ran), the verification nudge (files modified, nothing run afterward), and premature-claim suppression (`claimsAction`). Test against fabrication explicitly after any prompt or loop change.
4. **Built-in compound tools must stay disabled in the agent loop** (`enabledTools: []`) or compound's server-side ReAct loop intercepts the conversation. Web access goes through the local `web_search` tool, which one-shots compound-mini WITH built-ins enabled.
5. **Non-zero bash exit must throw** (status: error) — silent failure re-enables fabricated success claims.

## Rules

- Real implementations only. No placeholders, no TODO stubs, no mock data presented as real.
- Type-check (`bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`) must pass clean before declaring done.

- Logging is mandatory: every new event type goes through `logger.ts`, every agent-visible event also through `diagnostics.trace`.
- Diagnostics are local-only by design ("the most secure transport is no transport"). Never add a network sink.

## Final checklist

1. tsc clean.
2. Headless e2e run (simple + one failure-mode task) with filesystem-verified results.
3. TUI smoke test in tmux if UI was touched.

# ✦ glint

**A tiny agent that punches above its weight.** Free, terminal-native coding agent by [Glint Research](https://huggingface.co/Glint-Research).

```
❯ glint
              G L I N T   R E S E A R C H
                we teach tiny neural networks to think
```

glint is an inline TUI agent in the classic style — your scrollback stays yours. It reads, writes, edits, greps, runs shells, searches the web, remembers across sessions, and verifies its own work. Powered by `groq/compound` on Groq's free tier: **$0.00, forever.**

## Install

```bash
# needs bun ≥ 1.3 and imagemagick (logo build)
bun install
bun run build
cp dist/glint ~/.local/bin/
```

Single compiled binary. No Node, no Python, no runtime to babysit.

## Use

```bash
glint                      # interactive TUI (logo intro and all)
glint -p "fix the tests"   # headless one-shot
glint --yolo               # auto-approve tool actions
glint --no-intro           # skip the animation
glint --resume <id>        # continue a saved session
```

## Why it doesn't lie to you

Small models fabricate. glint's engine has four guards baked in:

1. **Reality check** — a final answer claiming actions when zero tools ran gets bounced back.
2. **Verification check** — file edits with no subsequent run demand proof before concluding.
3. **Failure-denial check** — "all tests pass" right after a failing command gets rejected.
4. **Premature-claim suppression** — success narration emitted before results land is held back.

When something still slips through, the TUI warns you instead of pretending.

## Features

| | |
|---|---|
| **Effort modes** | `/effort low · medium · high · max` — 6 to 50 tool rounds per turn |
| **Tools** | read, write, edit, ls, glob, grep (ripgrep), bash, web search, subagent |
| **Approvals** | writes & shell ask first with preview; read-only commands sail through; `/yolo` to trust |
| **Memory** | `remember` persists facts to `~/.glint/memory.md`, loaded every session |
| **Skills** | save workflows as `/name` commands; glint can mint them itself (`create_skill`) |
| **Subagents** | delegation to `groq/compound-mini` with read-only tools |
| **Sessions** | autosave, `/sessions`, `/resume`, auto-compaction near the context limit |
| **Project aware** | reads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` from your cwd into context; `/init` writes one |
| **Shell passthrough** | `!cmd` runs directly, output joins the agent's context |
| **Diagnostics** | SHA-256 hash-chained JSONL traces, local-only, `/diagnostics` to inspect, `/no-diagnostics` to opt out |
| **Logging** | everything to `~/.glint/logs/`, structured JSON lines |

## The trace vault

Every agent event (turns, tool calls, API timings, approvals) is appended to `~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl` with `0600` perms. Each record carries the SHA-256 of the previous record — edit or delete any line and `/diagnostics` reports the chain broken. Nothing is ever transmitted anywhere: *the most secure transport is no transport.*

```bash
jq . ~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-*.jsonl | less   # review your agent's history
```

## Engine notes

`groq/compound` has no custom function calling, so glint speaks a text tool protocol (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`) and parses both the canonical XML form and the model's drift variants — including calls the model "performs" inside its reasoning channel (salvaged, deduped per turn). Compound's server-side tools stay disabled in the agent loop; web access goes through a dedicated tool that one-shots `compound-mini` with built-in search.

See [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for the full contract if you (or your agent) work on this codebase.

---

*"We teach tiny neural networks to think. Sometimes they surprise us. Sometimes they just output zeros."*

---
name: groq-compound-quirks
description: groq/compound API behaviors that break agent loops — no custom tools, reasoning-channel execution, fabrication
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`groq/compound` (Groq, free tier) quirks discovered building [[glint-cli-project]]:

- **No custom function calling** — only built-in tools (web_search, code_interpreter, visit_website). Text tool protocols are the workaround.
- `compound_custom: {tools: {enabled_tools: []}}` disables its server-side ReAct loop; leaving built-ins on makes it intercept/execute things itself ("invalid command type, must be one of: search, visit").
- Exposes a `reasoning` field; the model frequently "performs" text-protocol tool calls inside reasoning and never repeats them in content — and then re-emits them every round (needs per-turn dedup).
- Fabricates aggressively: claims file creation/test passes that never happened. Needs reality/verification/failure-denial guards plus claims-suppression.
- Model drifts between tool-block formats (XML tags vs sentinels) — parse all variants.
- Endpoint accepts standard chat.completions + streaming SSE; usage in final chunk under `usage` or `x_groq.usage`; `usage_breakdown` lists underlying models (llama-4-scout, gpt-oss-120b).

:salute: Everything done. All 8 steps complete, tested, verified.

## glint v1.0.0 — shipped

**Run it:** `glint` (installed at `~/.local/bin/glint`, 104MB single binary, no runtime). `glint -p "task"` for headless. Source: `/home/lane/GR/glint-cli`, website: `/home/lane/GR/site/index.html`.

**What got built, in order:**

1. **Researched** Glint Research HF org (orange #F97316, Cinzel, dark, "we teach tiny neural networks to think"), agent TUI patterns from Claude Code/opencode/Codex, and Hermes Agent.
2. **Engine** — Bun + TypeScript + Ink inline TUI (classic scrollback style, no alt-screen). groq/compound hardcoded, compound-mini for subagents.
3. **Big discovery:** compound has **no custom function calling** — built text tool protocol instead. Model also "executes" tools inside its reasoning channel and **fabricates results** ("2.5M ssh pubkeys" — invented). Built 5 guards: reasoning-channel salvage + dedup, reality nudge, verification nudge, failure-denial nudge, stall nudge. After hardening: complex multi-bug fix task passes with **filesystem-independent verification** (`ALL TESTS PASS` confirmed by me, not the model).
4. **Logo intro** — embedme.html SVG rasterized to braille Unicode via ImageMagick at build time; terminal port of the outside-in stroke draw, light sweep, letter-cascade wordmark with orange GLINT shimmer. Any key skips, `--no-intro` flag, `/intro` replays.
5. **Diagnostics** — hyper-secure means *no transport*: SHA-256 hash-chained JSONL at `~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-*.jsonl`, 0600 perms, tamper-evident (`/diagnostics` verifies — 318 records, chain intact). `/no-diagnostics` opts out. Everything also logged to `~/.glint/logs/`.
6. **Hermes features added** — persistent memory (`remember` tool + `/memory`), agent-minted skills (`create_skill` → `/name` commands, tested live), subagent delegation, `!cmd` shell passthrough, sessions with `/resume` + auto-compaction.
7. **Effort modes** — `/effort low/medium/high/max` (6→50 tool rounds), in the status bar.
8. **Website** — Glint Research style with the actual animated logo embed, fake-terminal demo reproducing a real session, feature grid. Screenshots attached.

Tested: simple file tasks, multi-bug debug loops, web search (correct with citations), skill create/invoke, interrupt, approvals, resume, compact, double-ctrl-C, opt-out — all in tmux against the compiled binary. `AGENTS.md` (MythosMini-style contract) documents the five hard constraints for future agents.

# ✦ glint

**A tiny agent that punches above its weight.** Free, terminal-native coding agent by [Glint Research](https://huggingface.co/Glint-Research).

```
❯ glint
              G L I N T   R E S E A R C H
                we teach tiny neural networks to think
```

glint is an inline TUI agent in the classic style — your scrollback stays yours. It reads, writes, edits, greps, runs shells, searches the web, remembers across sessions, and verifies its own work. Powered by `groq/compound` on Groq's free tier: **$0.00, forever.**

## Install

```bash
# needs bun ≥ 1.3 and imagemagick (logo build)
bun install
bun run build
cp dist/glint ~/.local/bin/
```

Single compiled binary. No Node, no Python, no runtime to babysit.

## Use

```bash
glint                      # interactive TUI (logo intro and all)
glint -p "fix the tests"   # headless one-shot
glint --yolo               # auto-approve tool actions
glint --no-intro           # skip the animation
glint --resume <id>        # continue a saved session
```

## Why it doesn't lie to you

Small models fabricate. glint's engine has four guards baked in:

1. **Reality check** — a final answer claiming actions when zero tools ran gets bounced back.
2. **Verification check** — file edits with no subsequent run demand proof before concluding.
3. **Failure-denial check** — "all tests pass" right after a failing command gets rejected.
4. **Premature-claim suppression** — success narration emitted before results land is held back.

When something still slips through, the TUI warns you instead of pretending.

## Features

| | |
|---|---|
| **Effort modes** | `/effort low · medium · high · max` — 6 to 50 tool rounds per turn |
| **Tools** | read, write, edit, ls, glob, grep (ripgrep), bash, web search, subagent |
| **Approvals** | writes & shell ask first with preview; read-only commands sail through; `/yolo` to trust |
| **Memory** | `remember` persists facts to `~/.glint/memory.md`, loaded every session |
| **Skills** | save workflows as `/name` commands; glint can mint them itself (`create_skill`) |
| **Subagents** | delegation to `groq/compound-mini` with read-only tools |
| **Sessions** | autosave, `/sessions`, `/resume`, auto-compaction near the context limit |
| **Project aware** | reads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` from your cwd into context; `/init` writes one |
| **Shell passthrough** | `!cmd` runs directly, output joins the agent's context |
| **Diagnostics** | SHA-256 hash-chained JSONL traces, local-only, `/diagnostics` to inspect, `/no-diagnostics` to opt out |
| **Logging** | everything to `~/.glint/logs/`, structured JSON lines |

## The trace vault

Every agent event (turns, tool calls, API timings, approvals) is appended to `~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl` with `0600` perms. Each record carries the SHA-256 of the previous record — edit or delete any line and `/diagnostics` reports the chain broken. Nothing is ever transmitted anywhere: *the most secure transport is no transport.*

```bash
jq . ~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-*.jsonl | less   # review your agent's history
```

## Engine notes

`groq/compound` has no custom function calling, so glint speaks a text tool protocol (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`) and parses both the canonical XML form and the model's drift variants — including calls the model "performs" inside its reasoning channel (salvaged, deduped per turn). Compound's server-side tools stay disabled in the agent loop; web access goes through a dedicated tool that one-shots `compound-mini` with built-in search.

See [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for the full contract if you (or your agent) work on this codebase.

---

*"We teach tiny neural networks to think. Sometimes they surprise us. Sometimes they just output zeros."*

# AGENTS.md — Operating Rules for AI Agents in glint-cli

glint is a free agent CLI by Glint Research: a Bun + TypeScript + Ink TUI that drives groq/compound through a text tool protocol. This file is the contract for any agent working in this repository. Read it fully before changing anything.

## Commands

```bash
bun install                  # install dependencies
bun run dev                  # run the TUI from source
bun run src/index.tsx -p "task" --yolo   # headless one-shot (the e2e test entry)
bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit       # type check — must stay clean
bun run build                # regenerate logo + compile dist/glint
bun run install-bin          # install dist/glint to ~/.local/bin
```

All of these must keep working with no arguments and no manual setup. If your change affects any of them, rerun the affected one in the same session and prove it.

## Architecture (read before editing)

- `src/core/` — engine, no UI imports allowed here:
  - `groq.ts` streaming client (retries, SSE) · `protocol.ts` tool-block parsing (XML + sentinel forms)
  - `agent.ts` the loop: reasoning-channel salvage, turn-scoped dedup, reality/verification nudges
  - `tools.ts` tool registry · `prompts.ts` system prompt · `compact.ts` history compaction
  - `diagnostics.ts` hash-chained local JSONL traces · `logger.ts` file log · `session.ts`/`memory.ts`/`skills.ts` persistence
- `src/tui.tsx` + `src/components/` — Ink UI. Transcript via `<Static>`, dynamic region below.
- `src/generated/logo.ts` — generated by `scripts/build-logo.ts` from `../embedme.html`. Never edit by hand.
- `src/headless.ts` — `-p` one-shot mode used for e2e testing.

## Hard-won constraints (violate these and the agent breaks)

1. **groq/compound has NO custom function calling.** Tools work via text blocks (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`). The model drifts between formats — `protocol.ts` parses both XML and `<<<glint:tool` sentinel forms. Keep both.
2. **The model "executes" tools inside its reasoning channel.** `agent.ts` salvages calls from `res.reasoning`, deduped per turn (`turnExecuted`). Removing the dedup causes infinite re-execution loops; removing the salvage makes the agent claim work it never did.
3. **The model fabricates.** Three guards exist: the reality nudge (final answer claims actions, zero tools ran), the verification nudge (files modified, nothing run afterward), and premature-claim suppression (`claimsAction`). Test against fabrication explicitly after any prompt or loop change.
4. **Built-in compound tools must stay disabled in the agent loop** (`enabledTools: []`) or compound's server-side ReAct loop intercepts the conversation. Web access goes through the local `web_search` tool, which one-shots compound-mini WITH built-ins enabled.
5. **Non-zero bash exit must throw** (status: error) — silent failure re-enables fabricated success claims.

## Rules

- Real implementations only. No placeholders, no TODO stubs, no mock data presented as real.
- Type-check (`bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`) must pass clean before declaring done.
- Every engine change gets an e2e proof: run a headless task that exercises it and verify the filesystem outcome independently — do not trust the agent's own claims (see constraint 3).
- TUI changes get a tmux proof: launch in tmux, send keys, capture-pane, read the render.
- Keep `src/core/` free of UI imports; keep UI free of direct Groq calls.
- The API key and model names in `config.ts` are hardcoded by explicit project requirement; env `GROQ_API_KEY` overrides. Do not "fix" this.
- Logging is mandatory: every new event type goes through `logger.ts`, every agent-visible event also through `diagnostics.trace`.
- Diagnostics are local-only by design ("the most secure transport is no transport"). Never add a network sink.

## Final checklist

1. tsc clean.
2. Headless e2e run (simple + one failure-mode task) with filesystem-verified results.
3. TUI smoke test in tmux if UI was touched.
4. `bun run build` succeeds and `dist/glint --version` works if anything under `src/` changed.
5. No placeholder text, no dead code, no claims without proof.

content.text:
Both fixed, rebuilt, and verified live.

**View snapping — root cause found and fixed.** The input bar was unmounting whenever a turn started and remounting when it ended, so the whole layout jumped twice per turn. Now:

- The input bar is **permanently mounted at the bottom** — transcript, stream, thinking, approval, effort menu, TODOs, and the spinner all stack above it; nothing ever replaces it.
- Bonus that falls out of this: you can **type while the agent works** — mid-run submissions queue with a `◦ queued — sends when this turn finishes` notice and auto-send when the turn ends (verified: asked a second question mid-search, it queued and ran itself).
- Two more flicker sources fixed: streaming now repaints on a ~120ms tick instead of per-token (fast generations were forcing dozens of full relayouts per second), and the live regions are height-capped (stream to 14 lines, expanded thinking to 12) so they can't overflow the terminal and shove the layout around.
- When an approval or the effort menu has focus, the input stays visible but dims and ignores keys — confirmed `y` goes to the approval dialog, not the text box.

**Escalating reasoning per effort level.** Each level's prompt now demands strictly more deliberate thinking than the one below it:

- **low** — think only as much as strictly needed, one-line plan, act.
- **medium** — step-by-step before each action: what I know, what I need, why this action; check results against expectations.
- **high** — per-step protocol: restate the goal, list ≥2 candidate approaches, justify the pick, predict the outcome, and stop to re-derive on any prediction mismatch.
- **max** — full deliberation: decompose by dependency, multiple hypotheses per subproblem, adversarially attack your own favorite until it survives, reconcile every surprise, then a final self-review pass over everything produced.
- **ultracode** — everything from max plus the orchestration loop (plan → todos → delegate → work-while-they-work → verify), unlimited rounds, and "distrust your own success claims until proven by a run."

Type-checked, compiled, and the binary at `~/.local/bin/glint` is current — relaunch your session to pick it up.

✦ AI Archives – Detailed Project Description

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  1. High‑level Summary
  AI Archives is a Node.js web application built with Express that serves as a lightweight portal for storing, browsing, and running archived AI‑related “games” or
  interactive demos. It provides a static front‑end UI, a JSON API for retrieving archive metadata, and the ability to launch separate game servers for each archive entry.
   When run with the --host flag (or the HOSTING environment variable), it also creates public tunnels via cloudflared, exposing both the main portal and each game server
  to the internet.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

   │ │

   │ │   └─ <entry-id>/        ← each entry has its own folder

  5. How the System Works at Runtime

  1. Startup
      ◦ npm start → node server/index.js → listen(PORT) (default 4000).
      ◦ If the chosen port is busy, the server automatically increments and retries.

  2. Portal URL
      ◦ In normal mode: http://localhost:<actualPort> is printed.
      ◦ In hosting mode: a Cloudflare tunnel is created for the portal itself, and a public URL like https://xxxx.trycloudflare.com is displayed.

  3. Archive Discovery
      ◦ loadEntries() reads each archive.json under archives/.
      ◦ Each entry may specify a custom port; otherwise the server assigns sequential ports starting at 3001.

  4. Game Server Launch
      ◦ For every entry that contains an app/server/index.js, a child Node process is spawned on its assigned port.
      ◦ Output from each game server is prefixed with [<entry-id>] for easy identification.

  5. Optional Tunneling for Games
      ◦ When hosting, startTunnel(port) is called for each game server’s port, producing a public URL that is stored in tunnelUrls.
      ◦ mapEntryUrl(entry) injects that URL into the entry’s JSON response, allowing the front‑end to link directly to the public game instance.

  6. API Consumption
      ◦ The front‑end (served from public/) fetches /api/entries to display a list of archives, each with a title, date, and (if hosting) a public URL.
      ◦ Clicking an entry can open its game server (local or public) or display additional metadata.

  7. Static Archive Access
      ◦ The route /archives/<entry-id>/… serves raw files from the archive folder, enabling direct download of assets or data.

  8. Shutdown
      ◦ On SIGINT/SIGTERM, cleanup() kills all child processes, ensuring no orphaned game servers or tunnels remain.

   │

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  8. Extensibility Points

  1. Add New Archives – Drop a new folder under archives/ with an archive.json and optional app/ containing a game server. The portal will automatically detect and launch
  it on next start.
  2. Custom Proxy Rules – Use http-proxy-middleware to forward specific routes to external services (e.g., AI model APIs).
  3. Front‑end Enhancements – The public/ directory can be replaced with any SPA framework (React, Vue, Svelte) that consumes the /api/entries endpoint.
  4. Authentication – Add middleware to protect the API or static assets if needed.
  5. Persisted State – Store runtime data (e.g., tunnel URLs) in a lightweight DB or JSON file for later retrieval.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  9. Summary

  AI Archives is a modular, self‑hosting portal that:

  • Lists AI‑related archive entries (metadata stored in JSON).
  • Serves a static front‑end UI for browsing those entries.
  • Spawns independent Node.js game servers for each entry, each on its own port.
  • Optionally exposes both the portal and each game server publicly via Cloudflare tunnels.

  The codebase is concise, relies on well‑known Node.js libraries, and is designed for easy extension—new archives can be added simply by dropping a folder with the
  required structure, and the server will automatically discover and run them.

  The repository is a small‑to‑medium Node.js web application that serves static front‑end assets and provides a JSON API via an Express server. It follows a conventional
  layout:

   ┌
   │ /home/lane/AIArchives

  • Reads the listening port from config/default.json.

  Modularity

  • Routes are split into separate files for clarity (api.js, auth.js).
  • Middleware holds reusable functions (e.g., logging, error handling).
  • Config isolates environment‑specific values from code.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  3. `public/` – Front‑end Assets

   ┌
   │ public/
   │ ├─ index.html        # Main page served to browsers
   │ ├─ styles/
   │ │   └─ main.css      # Global stylesheet
   │ ├─ scripts/
   │ │   └─ app.js        # Front‑end JavaScript (likely calls the API)
   │ └─ assets/
   │     ├─ logo.png
   │     └─ favicon.ico
   └

  • Served as static content via express.static('public').
  • app.js probably performs fetch calls to the /api endpoints defined in the backend.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  4. `archives/` – Historical Data

   ┌
   │ archives/
   │ ├─ 2023-12-01-backup.zip
   │ ├─ old-config.json
   │ └─ logs/
   │     └─ server-2023-11.log
   └

  • Stores backups, previous configuration snapshots, and log files.
  • Not part of the runtime but useful for maintenance, debugging, or rollback.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  5. Development & Deployment Workflow

   ┌─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ npm script  │ What it does                                                       │ 
   ├─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ npm run dev │ Starts the server with nodemon for live reload during development. │ 
   │ npm start   │ Runs the production‑ready server (node server/index.js).           │ 
   │ npm test    │ Executes the Mocha test suite (mocha).                             │ 
   └─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Developers can edit code in server/ and public/, run npm run dev to see changes instantly, and add tests under a test/ folder (not shown but implied by the mocha
  script).

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  6. Potential Extensions

  • Database integration – Add a models/ directory with ORM/ODM (e.g., Sequelize, Mongoose) and configure connection strings in config/default.json.
  • Environment variables – Use dotenv to keep secrets out of source control.
  • Enhanced testing – Expand the Mocha/Chai suite to cover route handlers, middleware, and front‑end API interactions.
  • CI/CD – Set up GitHub Actions or similar to run npm ci && npm test on each push, ensuring deterministic builds via package-lock.json.
  • Dockerization – Create a Dockerfile to containerize the app for consistent deployment.

  ────────────────────────────────────────

  7. Summary

  The project is a Node.js/Express web application with a clear separation of concerns:

  • Backend (`server/`) handles API logic, middleware, and configuration.
  • Frontend (`public/`) provides static HTML/CSS/JS that consumes the API.
  • Archives (`archives/`) keep historical artifacts and logs.

  It is ready for further feature development, testing, and deployment, following standard Node.js conventions.

**TPS arrow.** It was comparing 10s windows — early in any turn the previous window was always empty, so the arrow froze on ↑. Now the rate is a 3-second average and the trend compares the last 3s against the 3s before it. Verified live: ↑287 → ↓91 → ↑224 across one generation.

**Bottom lock — properly this time.** The previous fix only kept the input mounted; the region still floated up under the transcript. Now the dynamic area spans the full terminal height with a spacer in the middle, so the input bar and the status text under it are physically pinned to the last rows of the screen — fresh session, mid-stream, idle, always. The transcript shows its most recent tail directly above the input (an oversized answer shows `✦ …` plus its last lines, with the complete copy already flushed to your terminal's scrollback), and older items flow up into scrollback as new ones arrive. Stream capping is now wrap-aware and the region hard-clips, which also killed the line-corruption artifacts I caught mid-stream during testing.
